description: Small offline knowledge base used to answer ASK_QUESTION queries when no conversational AI provider is configured. Retrieval uses TF-IDF cosine similarity; extend by adding entries.

entries.title: Machine learning
entries.answer: Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence where computers learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules. A model is trained on examples, measured on data it hasn't seen, and then used to make predictions on new inputs. I use machine learning myself to recognise what you want from your sentences.

entries.title: Artificial intelligence
entries.answer: Artificial intelligence is the field of building systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognising images, planning and making decisions. Modern AI combines techniques like machine learning, search, logic and probabilistic reasoning.

entries.title: Difference between AI and machine learning
keywords: difference between ai and machine learning
entries.answer: Artificial intelligence is the broad goal of making machines behave intelligently. Machine learning is one way to achieve it: instead of programming every rule, you let the system learn rules from data. Deep learning is in turn a subset of machine learning that uses large neural networks.

entries.title: Neural networks
keywords: how does a neural network learn
entries.answer: A neural network is a model made of layers of simple units called neurons. Each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs and applies a non-linear function. The network learns by adjusting its weights with backpropagation and gradient descent so that its predictions get closer to the correct answers.

entries.title: Deep learning
entries.answer: Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers. Each layer learns increasingly abstract features, for example edges, then shapes, then objects in an image. It powers speech recognition, image recognition and large language models, but it usually needs a lot of data and computing power.

entries.title: Natural language processing
entries.answer: Natural language processing is the area of AI that lets computers work with human language. Typical tasks include tokenisation, intent classification, entity extraction, translation and summarisation. My own pipeline normalises your text, classifies its intent and then extracts entities like times and durations.

entries.title: TF-IDF
entries.answer: TF-IDF stands for term frequency times inverse document frequency. It turns text into numbers by giving a word a high weight when it appears often in a sentence but rarely across the whole dataset, so distinctive words like timer or weather matter more than common words like the.

entries.title: Logistic regression
entries.answer: Logistic regression is a linear classification model. It computes a weighted score for each class and converts the scores into probabilities with the logistic or softmax function. It's fast, works well with TF-IDF features and is easy to interpret, which is why I use it to classify your intents.

entries.title: Intelligent agent
entries.answer: An intelligent agent perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators to achieve goals. I'm a simple example: I perceive your speech, decide what you want using a trained model and confidence rules, and then act by setting timers, reminders or answering.

entries.title: Supervised learning
entries.answer: Supervised learning trains a model on labelled examples, meaning each input comes with the correct answer. The model learns to map inputs to outputs and is evaluated on a held-out test set. My intent classifier is trained this way on sentences labelled with their intents.

entries.title: Unsupervised learning
entries.answer: Unsupervised learning finds structure in data without labels, for example grouping similar customers with clustering or compressing data with dimensionality reduction.

entries.title: Reinforcement learning
entries.answer: Reinforcement learning trains an agent by trial and error. The agent takes actions in an environment, receives rewards or penalties, and learns a policy that maximises its long-term reward. It is used in game playing, robotics and recommendation systems.

entries.title: Overfitting
entries.answer: Overfitting happens when a model memorises its training data, including the noise, and then performs poorly on new data. It's reduced with more data, regularisation, simpler models and validation techniques like cross-validation.

entries.title: Confusion matrix
entries.answer: A confusion matrix is a table that compares true labels with predicted labels. The diagonal counts correct predictions and the off-diagonal cells show which classes get confused with each other. You can see mine on the Analytics page.

entries.title: Precision, recall and F1
entries.answer: Precision is the share of predictions for a class that were correct. Recall is the share of real examples of that class that the model found. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of the two, which balances them in a single number.

entries.title: Large language models
keywords: what is a large language model
entries.answer: A large language model is a very large neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word. That simple objective lets it answer questions, summarise and write. Nova can optionally route open questions to such a model, but its command understanding uses its own lightweight classifier.

entries.title: Speech recognition
entries.answer: Speech recognition converts audio into text. The audio is split into short frames, turned into acoustic features, and a neural network predicts the most likely sequence of words. In Nova, your browser's speech recognition produces the transcript and my classifier takes it from there.

entries.title: Computer vision
entries.answer: Computer vision is the field of AI that lets computers understand images and video, for tasks such as object detection, face recognition and medical image analysis. Most modern systems use convolutional neural networks or vision transformers.

entries.title: Decision trees
entries.answer: A decision tree makes predictions by asking a sequence of yes-or-no questions about the input features, splitting the data at each step to make the groups purer. Random forests combine many trees to make predictions more accurate and stable.

entries.title: Why is the sky blue
entries.answer: The sky looks blue because of Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight contains all colours, but the tiny molecules in the air scatter short blue wavelengths much more than long red ones, so blue light reaches your eyes from every direction of the sky.

entries.title: Alan Turing
entries.answer: Alan Turing was a British mathematician who laid the foundations of computer science with the Turing machine, helped break the Enigma code in the Second World War, and proposed the Turing test as a way to ask whether machines can think.

entries.title: Python
entries.answer: Python is a popular high-level programming language known for readable syntax and a huge ecosystem of libraries. It's the most common language for data science and machine learning, and my backend is written in it using FastAPI and scikit-learn.

entries.title: About Nova
entries.answer: I'm Nova, a local voice assistant built as an AI and machine learning project. I understand your requests with my own trained intent classifier, and I can tell the time and date, do calculations, set timers and reminders, run focus sessions, open websites and check the weather.
